clinician.final_diagnosis: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM), triggered by recent viral illness
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 35-year-old male with chronic insomnia and persistent fatigue presented with a 1-week prodrome of severe headaches, arthralgias, and myalgias, initially diagnosed as upper respiratory tract infection at a local hospital. He subsequently developed severe throbbing headache with photophobia, phonophobia, and visual disturbances, misdiagnosed as complex migraine with nonspecific brain MRI findings and discharged. He returned 12 hours later with acute decreased consciousness (GCS 10/15), confusion, right eye swelling, tachycardia, decreased breath sounds, and signs of meningeal irritation. CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein with negative viral PCR (HSV) and negative bacterial cultures. Follow-up brain MRI demonstrated newly developed multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the left hemisphere, right parietal and temporal lobes with mild leptomeningeal enhancement, consistent with acute demyelination. The patient was treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, resulting in significant improvement in consciousness and orientation within 3 days. Treatment was continued with oral prednisolone taper (40 mg daily) over 4-6 weeks, supplemented with Haloperidol for agitation management and anticonvulsant therapy for seizure prophylaxis. At discharge, the patient had returned to full orientation with resolution of confusion and marked improvement in cognitive and motor functions, able to walk unassisted with only mild residual fatigue.
